question: Can a small case reveal work and taste without becoming a portrait of an entire reign?
summary: A painted case joins practical storage with skilled surface work. Its flowers, birds, mirror and compartments invite close observation, while the museum supplies its maker, date and intended dressing function. A separately dated account of Shiraz connects building, merchants and artisans without turning an Iranian object into evidence for everyone’s life or a named ruler’s possessions.

sections.title: Making a useful container
sections.text: The case combines a rectangular frame, a drawer and a removable lid covering a mirror. In the supplied photograph, birds and flowers cover the outer surface while a fitted drawer projects beside the frame. The museum describes compartments intended for dressing implements such as scissors, tweezers and a comb. Constructing storage and arranging a painted surface were related kinds of skilled work. The photograph reveals shapes and decoration; the catalogue explains the intended contents.

sections.title: Paint, support and protection
sections.text: The Met names Muhammad Baqir and identifies painted, lacquered papier-maché and pasteboard. These materials joined a container’s support with decorated surfaces. Columbia University’s exhibition on Persian bookbindings explains that thin varnish layers could provide a measure of protection, while wear remained possible. Its example is a later bookbinding, not an examination of this case. It helps explain why surface protection mattered without supplying this object’s exact recipe, pigments, working hours or condition.

sections.title: Building and working in Shiraz
sections.text: For the earlier political setting, historian John R. Perry describes Karim Khan’s residence at Shiraz from 1765 to 1779. A citadel, mosque, gardens and covered bazaar formed part of the building work. Merchants from Europe and India and artisans attracted from Isfahan contributed to the city’s activity. Such accounts connect court patronage with commercial and skilled work. They do not identify Muhammad Baqir’s workshop: the case’s catalogue gives Iran, without a secure city of manufacture.

sections.title: One object, several kinds of evidence
sections.text: The catalogue dates the case 1204 AH/1789 CE, ten years after Karim Khan’s death. It also describes an inner-lid courtly gathering. That gathering is absent from the three supplied views; readers can observe the outer decoration, mirror and drawer instead. Date, practical function and painted subject each support a different question. None identifies a purchaser or proves personal use by a ruler. The independently dated political reference keeps the later case connected to change without inventing ownership.

deeperReading.title: An intended use is not a surviving inventory
deeperReading.text: The catalogue’s description of a dressing set connects the fitted compartments with implements. The supplied alternate view shows empty recesses; it does not establish which particular tools once lay there, who handled them or how often. Likewise, the maker’s name identifies the museum’s catalogue attribution without recovering every person involved in preparing supports, painting or finishing. A later bookbinding account can explain a general role for varnish, but it is not a chemical study of these surfaces. Object-specific technical questions remain open.

deeperReading.title: Urban work and a courtly recollection
deeperReading.text: Perry’s account presents commercial arrangements and building alongside military authority. Karim Khan’s title wakil, or deputy, did not make the government a modern elected system or extend its control uniformly across Iran. A favorable recollection by Abd al-Razzaq Donboli offers a particular observer’s later memory of the Shiraz court. Donboli had been a hostage and guest, and later wrote in a Qajar setting. His voice can illuminate a remembered courtly atmosphere without establishing equal prosperity for merchants, artisans, servants or other residents. Their working conditions need further evidence.

evidenceReading.title: Visible parts, catalogue claims and political recollection
evidenceReading.introduction: These observations and editorial paraphrases distinguish the unchanged supplied views from catalogue information and a historian’s account. They are not a new technical examination or translation of an inscription.

items.label: A mirror and fitted storage support a practical question
items.text: The photographs show outer birds and flowers, a mirror and an empty fitted drawer. The catalogue connects the compartments with a dressing set.
items.interpretation: An observation about shapes can be checked in the supplied images. Intended use needs the catalogue. The photographed empty drawer does not recover its original tools, owner or daily routine. The catalogue-described inner-lid gathering is not visible in these three views.

items.label: A material name does not supply an exact recipe
items.text: The Met identifies painted and lacquered papier-maché and pasteboard. Columbia’s later bookbinding example explains a general relationship between support, varnish and limited protection.
items.interpretation: The catalogue supports the material identification; the comparison explains a possible function of surface protection. It does not establish this case’s exact layers, ingredients, pigments, condition or division of workshop labor.

items.label: A favorable court memory has a particular speaker
items.text: Perry attributes a pleasant recollection of Karim Khan’s court to Donboli, a former hostage and guest who later wrote in a Qajar setting.
items.interpretation: The recollection can be evidence for how one observer remembered the court. It cannot establish that every worker prospered. The independent 1779 death and 1789 object dates also prevent assigning the later case to Karim Khan without separate provenance.

familyActivity.title: What can the case itself show?
steps: Find a bird or flower, the mirror and the projecting drawer in the supplied photograph. Describe where each is without guessing an owner.
If alternate views are available, inspect the empty compartments. If they are not, use the source capsule’s description; no unseen detail is required.
Make two short claims: one based on a visible part, and one about intended use based on the catalogue. Explain which source supports each.
Read the two dates in the capsule. Explain why the case’s maker and date do not show that Karim Khan owned it. Add one unanswered question about its use.
familyActivity.explanation: Source capsule — editorial paraphrase: the museum names Muhammad Baqir and dates this Iranian case 1204 AH/1789 CE. It describes a mirror and compartments intended for dressing implements such as scissors, tweezers and a comb. The supplied photograph shows outer flowers and birds, a mirror and a drawer; an alternate view shows empty compartments. The catalogue also describes a courtly gathering on another surface, which these three supplied views do not show. Karim Khan died in 1779. The record does not establish a purchaser, personal use by that ruler or a secure Shiraz workshop.

review.reviewer: Codex selected source consultation and internal author QA; not independent historian or community approval
review.scope: A focused lacquer-object inquiry, practical activity and independently dated political reference. The original case, claims, media identity, whole date, rights, order and image bytes remain intact. Selected image descriptions are corrected separately after direct inspection: the catalogue-described inner-lid gathering is absent from the three supplied photographs.
limitations: The three supplied views omit the catalogue-described inner-lid courtly gathering. This is made explicit in the new reading and activity; no new image, visual detail or ownership is invented.

The later bookbinding source supplies general material context, not an exact recipe or examination of this case. Original inscriptions, underlying memoirs and agreements, purchaser, complete workshop team and current remote-image parity were not established.

The complete 1751–1794 case is distinct from the selected 1747–1794 reference, Karim Khan’s 1765–1779 residence and the 1789 object. Shiraz remains political context rather than a verified manufacturing location.
Independent specialist/community review, family use, human accessibility and physical print acceptance remain open.
